1

The petitioner was convicted and sentenced for the offence under Sections 16(1)(a)(i) r/w Section 7(2) r/w Section 2(9)(k) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 and Rule 32(b)(2) and 32(f) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955.
The conviction and sentence imposed by the trial Court was confirmed by the appellate Court also.
Challenging the same, this Criminal Revision has been filed.

2. Though very many contentions were urged by the petitioner's counsel, he submitted that he would be satisfied, if the Court adopts the same approach as adopted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Crl.A.No.214 of 2016.

In the said Judgment, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that even though the minimum term of imprisonment is contemplated in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954,
the new Act contemplates only levy of fine.
There is no minimum term of imprisonment provided in the new Act.
The Hon'ble Supreme Court took a view that the benefit in the new Act can be given even in the pending prosecution under the old Act.
In this case, the petitioner has been levied with 3 http://www.judis.nic.in months Simple Imprisonment as well as fine.
The fine amount has already been paid.
The learned counsel appearing for the petitioner submitted that he would be satisfied, if the sentence is set aside.
3. The petitioner is a lady.
She must be now aged around 65 years.
It is also seen that the manufacturer was not arrayed as an accused.
Taking note of these aspects, this Court even while maintaining the conviction imposed on the petitioner, sets aside the sentence of imprisonment.
It is made clear that this order will not come in the way of the petitioner in applying for any license under the Food Safety Act.
4. With this observation, the Criminal Revision stands partly allowed.
No costs.
